Separation of Mixtures and Purification.intro: A mixture contains two or more substances physically combined; its components retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods. A pure substance has a fixed composition and characteristic properties.

blocks.x: Choose a technique from differences in particle size, solubility, boiling point, volatility, magnetism or affinity for a surface. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; evaporation/crystallization recovers dissolved solids; simple distillation recovers a solvent or separates liquids with widely different boiling points; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with closer boiling points. A separating funnel handles immiscible liquids. Sublimation separates a sublimable solid. Chromatography separates substances by different attractions to stationary and mobile phases; Rf = distance travelled by spot/distance travelled by solvent front.

To separate sand and salt: add water to dissolve salt, filter off sand, wash and dry the residue, then evaporate the filtrate carefully to crystallize salt. To obtain pure water as well, distil the filtrate and collect the distillate.

Chemical Combination.intro: Chemical combination describes how elements and compounds react in fixed proportions to form new substances. Equations summarize reactants, products and conservation of atoms.

blocks.x: The law of conservation of mass says total mass is conserved in a closed chemical reaction. Definite proportions: a pure compound contains its elements in a fixed mass ratio. Multiple proportions: when two elements form several compounds, masses combining with a fixed mass of one element are in simple whole-number ratios. Relative atomic mass Ar and relative formula mass Mr have no units; amount n=m/M and particle count N=nNA, where NA≈6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. Balance equations by changing coefficients, never subscripts.
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O conserves four H atoms and two O atoms on both sides. For 18 g water, n=m/Mr=18/18=1 mol.

Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws.intro: The kinetic particle model explains states of matter and gas behaviour using moving particles. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of particles.

blocks.x: Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; liquid particles remain close but move past one another; gas particles are far apart and move randomly. Gas pressure comes from particle collisions with container walls. Boyle’s law pV=constant at fixed T; Charles’ law V/T=constant at fixed p; pressure law p/T=constant at fixed V. Combined law p₁V₁/T₁=p₂V₂/T₂; ideal gas equation pV=nRT. Use kelvin. Diffusion is faster at higher temperature and lower relative molecular mass; Graham’s law gives rate ∝1/√Mr.
A 2.0 L gas at 300 K is heated to 450 K at constant pressure: V₂=2.0×450/300=3.0 L.

Atomic Structure and Bonding.intro: Atoms contain a tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. Chemical bonding results from electrostatic attractions involving valence electrons and helps atoms reach more stable arrangements.

blocks.x: Protons have charge +1 and relative mass 1; neutrons charge 0 and mass 1; electrons charge −1 and tiny relative mass. Atomic number Z=protons; mass number A=protons+neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron numbers. Ionic bonding transfers electrons and creates oppositely charged ions; covalent bonding shares electron pairs; metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons. Bonding and structure explain properties: ionic solids conduct when molten/aqueous, metals conduct as solids, simple molecular substances often have low melting points.
For ²³₁₁Na, protons=11, electrons=11 in a neutral atom, neutrons=23−11=12. Sodium chloride forms Na⁺ and Cl⁻ by electron transfer.

Air.intro: Air is a mixture of gases, not a compound. Its composition is approximately constant in clean, dry lower-atmosphere air, though water vapour and pollutants vary.

blocks.x: Dry air contains about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, with trace gases. Oxygen supports combustion and respiration; nitrogen is relatively unreactive and used industrially to make ammonia; carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and contributes to the greenhouse effect. Air can be liquefied and separated by fractional distillation after purification and cooling. Combustion in sufficient oxygen usually gives CO₂ and H₂O for hydrocarbons; limited oxygen may produce CO or soot.
Complete combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. For 1 mol CH₄, 2 mol O₂ are required by the balanced equation.

Water.intro: Water is a polar covalent molecule and an effective solvent for many ionic and polar substances. Its unusual thermal and density properties are important in nature.

blocks.x: Pure water is H₂O; hydrogen bonding contributes to its high boiling point, surface tension and heat capacity. Water has maximum density near 4°C and expands on freezing. Hard water contains Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions: temporary hardness is commonly due to hydrogencarbonates and can be removed by boiling; permanent hardness from sulfates/chlorides can be softened chemically or by ion exchange. Potable water is safe for drinking, not necessarily chemically pure. Treatment can include sedimentation, filtration and disinfection.
Temporary hardness can be removed by heating: Ca(HCO₃)₂(aq) → CaCO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l). Insoluble CaCO₃ forms scale.

Solubility.intro: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.

blocks.x: Solubility is commonly expressed as grams of solute per 100 g solvent. An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; a saturated solution is at equilibrium with undissolved solute; a supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than normally stable and crystallizes readily. For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, but not always; gas solubility usually falls as temperature rises and increases with pressure. A solubility curve supports crystallization and mass calculations. Concentration c=n/V in mol dm⁻³, with V in dm³.
If 36 g of solute dissolves in 100 g water at a stated temperature, solubility is 36 g per 100 g water at that temperature.

Environmental Pollution.intro: Pollution occurs when harmful substances or energy enter the environment at levels that damage organisms or ecosystems. Chemistry helps identify pollutants, their sources and ways to reduce them.

blocks.x: Air pollutants include CO, SO₂, nitrogen oxides, particulates and excess greenhouse gases. SO₂ and NOx can form acid rain; particulates harm respiratory health; excess greenhouse gases enhance warming. Water pollutants include sewage, fertilizers, pesticides, oil and toxic metals. Nitrate/phosphate enrichment can cause eutrophication: algal growth, decomposition and oxygen depletion. Solid waste can be reduced by refusing, reducing, reusing and recycling. Pollution control targets source reduction, treatment and safe disposal.
Combustion of sulfur-containing fuel produces SO₂; oxidation and reaction with water can form acids that lower rainwater pH and damage ecosystems.

Acids, Bases and Salts.intro: Acids and bases are identified by how they behave in water and in reactions. Neutralization produces salt and water when an acid reacts with a base.

blocks.x: In aqueous solution, acids donate H⁺ (more accurately form H₃O⁺); bases accept H⁺, while alkalis are soluble bases producing OH⁻. Strong/weak refers to degree of ionization, not concentration. pH=−log₁₀[H⁺]; pH below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline at 25°C. Acid + metal → salt + H₂; acid + carbonate → salt + CO₂ + H₂O; acid + base/alkali → salt + water. Salt names depend on acid: hydrochloric → chloride; sulfuric → sulfate; nitric → nitrate. Titration determines reacting volumes/concentration.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. One mole sulfuric acid neutralizes two moles sodium hydroxide.

Oxidation and Reduction.intro: Redox reactions involve electron transfer or changes in oxidation number. Oxidation and reduction always occur together because electrons lost by one species are gained by another.

blocks.x: Oxidation can mean electron loss, oxidation-number increase or addition of oxygen/removal of hydrogen. Reduction means electron gain, oxidation-number decrease or removal of oxygen/addition of hydrogen. OIL RIG is a useful reminder: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons. Oxidizing agents accept electrons and are reduced; reducing agents donate electrons and are oxidized. Oxidation-number rules help identify redox: free elements 0, monatomic ions equal their charge, oxygen usually −2, hydrogen usually +1, and totals match the species charge.
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zn loses 2e⁻ and is oxidized; Cu²⁺ gains 2e⁻ and is reduced. Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent.

Electrolysis.intro: Electrolysis uses direct electric current to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change in a molten ionic compound or electrolyte solution.

blocks.x: The electrolyte contains mobile ions. Cations migrate to the cathode (negative electrode) and gain electrons; anions migrate to the anode (positive electrode) and lose electrons. Products depend on ions present, concentration and electrode type. In aqueous solutions, hydrogen may form instead of a reactive metal at the cathode; halides may be discharged at the anode when concentrated, otherwise oxygen can form. Faraday relation: Q=It; m=(MIt)/(zF), with F≈96,500 C mol⁻¹. In copper purification, impure copper is the anode and pure copper the cathode.
For Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, 2 mol electrons deposit 1 mol Cu. Charge for 1 mol Cu is 2F ≈193,000 C.

Energy Changes.intro: Chemical reactions involve energy changes as bonds break and form. Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy.

blocks.x: An exothermic reaction transfers heat to surroundings and has ΔH<0; an endothermic reaction absorbs heat and has ΔH>0. For bond enthalpies, ΔH≈Σ(bonds broken)−Σ(bonds formed). Reaction profiles show activation energy Ea and enthalpy change. A catalyst lowers activation energy but does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position. Calorimetry estimates heat change using q=mcΔT; molar enthalpy change is ΔH=−q/n for the reacting amount in a simple insulated experiment.
If breaking reactant bonds needs 800 kJ mol⁻¹ and forming product bonds releases 950 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH≈800−950=−150 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).

Rates of Chemical Reaction.intro: Reaction rate measures how quickly reactants are used or products are formed. Collision theory explains rate in terms of successful particle collisions.

blocks.x: Particles must collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy) and suitable orientation. Rate increases with concentration, gas pressure, temperature, surface area of a solid and addition of a suitable catalyst. A catalyst offers a lower-activation-energy pathway and is regenerated. Rate may be measured as amount or concentration change per time, gas volume per time, mass loss per time or colour change. On a concentration-time graph, gradient gives rate; the curve flattens as reactants are consumed.
Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than equal-mass chips with acid because more surface is exposed for collisions each second.

Chemical Equilibrium.intro: A reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a closed system when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Concentrations remain constant, but reactions continue microscopically.

blocks.x: For aA+bB ⇌ cC+dD, Kc=[C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations and omitting pure solids/liquids. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not change Kc or equilibrium composition. Le Chatelier’s principle: a system shifts to oppose an imposed concentration, pressure or temperature change. Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer gas moles; increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction. Only temperature changes Kc.
For N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward NH₃ because 2 gas moles are formed from 4 gas moles.

Non-Metals and Their Compounds.intro: Non-metals are generally poor conductors and tend to gain or share electrons, but their properties vary widely. Their compounds are central to air, water, agriculture and industry.

blocks.x: Hydrogen forms water and acids; oxygen supports combustion and forms oxides; nitrogen forms ammonia and nitrates; carbon forms CO₂, CO and an extensive range of covalent compounds; sulfur forms SO₂, SO₃ and sulfuric acid; chlorine forms chlorides and is a disinfectant. Many non-metal oxides are acidic and react with bases to form salts. Ammonia is a basic gas, highly soluble in water, and manufactured by the Haber process: N₂+3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (iron catalyst, elevated pressure and temperature as a compromise).
CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O; limewater turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms.

Metals and Their Compounds.intro: Metals generally conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and form positive ions. Their reactivity determines extraction methods and many displacement reactions.

blocks.x: The reactivity series commonly orders K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au from more to less reactive. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. Metals above carbon are often extracted by electrolysis; less reactive metals can often be reduced from oxides with carbon or carbon monoxide. Ores are concentrated, converted to suitable compounds and refined. Corrosion of iron needs oxygen and water; painting, oiling, galvanizing and sacrificial protection reduce it. Alloys alter properties by disrupting regular layers of metal atoms.
Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from solution.

Organic Compounds.intro: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Carbon forms four covalent bonds and long chains, rings and branched structures.

blocks.x: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated, general formula CnH₂n+₂; alkenes contain a C=C bond, formula CnH₂n for open-chain compounds, and undergo addition reactions. Functional groups determine characteristic reactions: alcohol −OH, carboxylic acid −COOH, ester −COO−. Homologous series members share a functional group and general formula; successive members differ by CH₂. Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity. Combustion, substitution, addition, polymerization and esterification are key reaction types.
Ethene adds bromine: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Bromine water changes from orange to colourless, testing for a carbon-carbon double bond.

Chemistry and Industry.intro: Chemical industries convert raw materials into useful products on large scales. Process design balances yield, rate, energy, safety, cost and environmental impact.

blocks.x: Important examples include Haber synthesis of ammonia, Contact-process manufacture of sulfuric acid, fractional distillation of crude oil, electrolysis of brine and extraction/refining of metals. Industrial decisions use equilibrium and rate principles: catalysts improve rate, higher pressure may improve gas yield but raises equipment cost, and temperature is chosen as a practical compromise. Atom economy = Mr of desired product/total Mr of products ×100%; percentage yield = actual yield/theoretical yield ×100%. Recycle unreacted feed where economical and control wastes and emissions.
Haber process: N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), exothermic; iron catalyst, elevated pressure, moderate temperature and recycling support efficient production.
